name: Rombo
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Rombo (romb1244) is not in the catalog. The sweep list had one item, Philippson 1991 (thesis, open full text at DDL Lyon; copy now under. Read in full text: Rombo ('chaga-est E 62c') is only inventoried in group XXI with a single + (limited data); all Chaga analysis (pp. 384-387, Annexe pp. 512-513) is for Vunjo, taken from McHugh 1990 — tone plus partially free lexical accent (penultimate of the theme for most themes) plus a demarcative length culmination — so it is a statement about another variety, silent on Rombo. The best first-hand statement on Rombo comes from material already on file from an earlier pass, verified here: Shinagawa 2021 (ILCAA, open access), p. 197 fn. 15, classifies Rombo as a tone language with weak accentual properties that fails Hyman's culminativity criterion, i.e. not a stress-accent language; no positional stress rule is given there, in Shinagawa 2014 (sketch sec. 1.4 p. 13) or in Philippson & Montlahuc 2003 (Mashati Rombo tone). Still unobtained: Montlahuc 2000 INALCO thesis on eastern Chaga (print only, not on HAL/theses.fr) and Shinagawa 2025 Oxford Guide chapter on Mkuu E623C (paywalled DOI 10.1093/oso/9780198808343.003.0070) — medium priority as possible first-hand accent statements for Rombo varieties. discovery went through on-disk copies, the DDL full-text server and theses.fr. updated (addendum stamped 2026-09-17T14:13:20Z).

earlier_scan.source_named: Montlahuc, Marie-Laure 2000. Elements de description du chaga-oriental. These, INALCO Paris. 332pp (long grammar of Rombo/Eastern Chaga); also McHugh 1987 sketch.

new_statements.quote: この必須性と唯一性（culminativity：語は「最大ひとつの」音調上のプロミネンスを有する＝複数のプロミネンスを有さない）を同時に満たすものが、典型的なstress accent言語であるというのが同論文の提案であるが、それに従えばロンボ語は前者は満たす（あくまでも単独形でということだが）ものの後者は満たさないという点で、アクセント性の弱いトーン言語（同論文の定義では、ピッチが形態素の語彙的な実現に何らかの形で関与している言語）と位置付けられることになる。
new_statements.translation: That paper's [Hyman 2006] proposal is that a language which satisfies both this obligatoriness and culminativity (culminativity: a word has 'at most one' tonal prominence, i.e. does not have multiple prominences) is a typical stress-accent language; following it, Rombo satisfies the former (though only in isolation forms) but not the latter, and is therefore to be classed as a tone language with weak accentual properties (in that paper's definition, a language in which pitch is involved in some way in the lexical realization of morphemes).
new_statements.citation: Shinagawa, Daisuke. 2021. Rombo-go (Bantu E623) no seichoo pataan gaikan [An overview of the tone patterns of Rombo (Bantu E623)]. In Kaji, Shigeki (ed.), Afurika shogo no seichoo, akusento [Tone and accent in African languages], ch. 9, pp. 177-208. Tokyo: ILCAA, Tokyo University of Foreign Studies.
new_statements.locator: p. 197, footnote 15 (sec. 2.6, discussion of table 8/9; PDF page 21 of the chapter file)
new_statements.reading: tone language with a stress statement
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (37 pp. 197 (header 'ロンボ語 197'). Footnote 15 reads exactly as quoted (only line breaks differ): 'この概念は、Hyman (2006) によるprosodic typologyの類型基準として提案されているものを援用したものである。同論文によれば、必須性とは語の中に「少なくとも一つの」音調上のプロミネンスを有するという性質である。この必須性と唯一性（culminativity：...）を同時に満たすものが、典型的なstress accent言語であるというのが同論文の提案であるが、それに従えばロンボ語は前者は満たす（あくまでも単独形でということだが）ものの後者は満たさないという点で、アクセント性の弱いトーン言語（...）と位置付けられることになる。' The footnote hangs on the sec. 2.6 sentence (p. 196-197, well-formedness constraints on underlying tone sequences, tables 8-9): the absence of isolation forms with no surface H at all (pattern 1-a) is interpreted as obligatoriness of H. Surrounding section is entirely about the four 2-syllable stem patterns (-ØØ/…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Rombo is a tone language (privative H vs. unmarked, syllable as TBU, surface H / upstepped super-high / downstepped H / L). It is explicitly not a stress-accent language: every word carries at least one H in isolation (obligatoriness), but words may carry more than one H (no culminativity), so no single culminative word prominence and no positional stress rule is given. Nouns in isolation avoid all-L patterns; before an associative all noun H's are neutralised to L. Affirmative main-clause verbs get a H on the first or second syllable (verb-initial H, IH), absent in negatives and subordinates.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned; the source describes multiple H tones per word, not stress levels.
new_statements.exceptions: Obligatoriness holds only in isolation forms; noun tone patterns show considerable free variation and neutralisation, especially among young speakers; verb stems sometimes behave as both H and L class; tone patterns are described as in progressive obscuring/simplification.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, citation (isolation) forms of nouns, plus phrase-level contexts (copula, negative ku, associative, possessive); the (non-)culminativity remark is about the word in isolation. Shinagawa 2014 sketch sec. 1.4 p. 13 adds only that Chaga languages in general are said to have complex tone (or accent) patterns, much obscured in present-day Rombo.
new_statements.identity_note: Shinagawa's Rombo data (2014 sketch, 2014 vocabulary, 2021 tone chapter) come from a variety he places on the Mkuu-Keni continuum of Rombo District (Maho E623C Mkuu / E623D Keni), i.e. South-Rombo in Philippson & Montlahuc's (2003) terms; Montlahuc's own Rombo research (reported second-hand in that chapter) is on the Mashati variety of North-Rombo, which lacks tone shift. Glottolog romb1244 covers Rombo as a whole; no separate glottocodes for these dialects were verified. McHugh 1987, listed by Glottolog under romb1244, is on Wunjo/Kivunjo (Central Chaga), not Rombo.

new_statements.translation: That paper [Hyman 2006] proposes that a language satisfying both obligatoriness and culminativity (a word has 'at most one' tonal prominence, i.e. no multiple prominences) is a typical stress-accent language; following it, Rombo satisfies the former (though only in isolation forms) but not the latter, and is therefore to be placed as a tone language with weak accentual properties (in that paper's definition, a language in which pitch is involved in some way in the lexical realization of morphemes).
new_statements.citation: Shinagawa, Daisuke. 2021. Rombo-go (Bantu E623) no seichō patān gaikan [An overview of the tone patterns of Rombo (Bantu E623)]. In Kaji, Shigeki (ed.), Afurika shogo no seichō, akusento [Tone and accent in African languages], ch. 9, pp. 177-208. Tokyo: ILCAA, Tokyo University of Foreign Studies (CC BY 4.0).
new_statements.reading: Rombo is a tone language (lexical H vs. toneless stems, with a 'PLH' prefix-H property and downstep/spreading), not a stress-accent language: words may carry more than one H prominence, so culminativity fails; obligatoriness holds only for isolation forms. No positional word-stress rule (penultimate or otherwise) is stated anywhere in the chapter, in Shinagawa's 2014 grammatical sketch (sec. 1.4, p. 13: all Chaga languages are said to have complex tone-or-accent patterns, much levelled in young speakers' Rombo), or in Philippson & Montlahuc 2003 (Mashati North-Rombo: SH/H/L contrast, no tone shift). Best coding for a stress catalog: tonal, no word stress reported (a phrase-final demarcative length culmination is attested for Chaga generally by Philippson 1991, but only for Vunjo).

sources.note: Whole chapter is on tone (privative H vs. unmarked, syllable TBU, super-high and downstep, post-lexical H insertion, verb-initial H). Fn. 15 p. 197 is the only stress statement: Rombo meets Hyman's (2006) obligatoriness (in isolation forms only) but not culminativity, so it is a tone language with weak accentual properties, not a stress-accent language. No positional stress rule.

sources.citation: Shinagawa, Daisuke. 2019. Rombo (E623). In Descriptive materials of morphosyntactic microvariation in Bantu, pp. 153-189. Tokyo: ILCAA (BaSIS). (English)
sources.note: Morphosyntactic parameter questionnaire; phoneme inventory and tone diacritics (high, super-high/upstepped, downstepped, falling, rising) in the dagger footnote p. 153. Nothing on stress.

sources.citation: Shinagawa, Daisuke & Monica Apolinari. 2014 [CiNii dates 2015]. Chaga=Rombo-go (Bantu E623) kiso goishuu = A basic vocabulary of Chaga-Rombo (Bantu E623). Tokyo: ILCAA, TUFS. (Japanese)
sources.note: Front matter 'Onchoo pataan ni tsuite' (pp. vi-x): noun surface tone patterns in five syntactic frames (isolation, after copula ni, before negative ku, before associative -a, before possessive -akwa), all neutralised to LLL before the associative; verb H/L class criteria. Tone unstable in young speakers. No stress statement.

sources.citation: Shinagawa, Daisuke. 2014. Chaga=Rombo-go (Bantu E623) bunpoo suketchi = A grammatical sketch of Chaga-Rombo (Bantu E623). Tokyo: ILCAA, TUFS. viii+145 pp. (Glottolog 552146; Japanese)
sources.note: Ch. 1 phonology: 1.3 syllable structure p. 12, 1.4 tone pp. 13-14. Says all Chaga languages are reported to have complex tone (or accent) patterns (cf. Nurse 1977) but in present-day young speakers' Rombo this is much obscured, lexical tone contrasts largely neutralised; gives four principles of H realisation (verb-initial H in affirmative main verbs, super-H, H before negative ku, context-dependent noun tone). Nothing on stress; no accent/prominence terms anywhere else (grepped).

sources.citation: Shinagawa, Daisuke. 2014. Vowel length and TMA micro-variation in Kilimanjaro Bantu. Asian and African Languages and Linguistics 9 (ILCAA). (English)
sources.note: Vowel-length contrast (Mkuu/Rombo data) and its morphological consequences; no stress or accent statement.

sources.citation: Philippson, Gerard & Marie-Laure Montlahuc. 2003. Kilimanjaro Bantu (E60 and E74). In Nurse & Philippson (eds), The Bantu Languages, 475-500. London: Routledge.
sources.note: Sec. 1.2 p. 475-476: Rombo (E62c) = South-Rombo, North-Rombo (Mashati, Useri varieties); 'practically nothing has ever been published on... the whole of R.'. Sec. 2 segmental phonology (vowel length, pp. 476-477). Sec. 3 Tone pp. 479-481: Montlahuc's research shows the Mashati variety of North-Rombo has no tone shift but has the three-way SH/H/L contrast; table 24.2 Mashati lexical tone; SH spreads leftwards to the first H. No stress or accent statement for Rombo (accent mentioned only for Wunjo per McHugh).
